In short, Oakeshott can be understood as a critic and deconstructionist of modernity—the modern project that we have been enslaved to since the “Enlightenment.” In “Rationalism and Politics,” the essay that gives the collection its title, Oakeshott examines the phenomenon of “rationalism” as the goal-oriented (ideological) direction of politics that has arisen in the modern West since the time of Machiavelli, Bacon, and Descartes. Essentially, the end result of rationalist politics is the destruction of hearth and home, of practical knowledge and the humanities, in the pursuit of a homogenous universal ideal guided by “The Book” (whether it be Machiavelli’s “Prince” or Marx’s “Das Kapital”). The rationalist is a mechanist who believes all things are like machines needing to be fine-tuned and solved.
